records.quote:
"The _padre_ say he no can help you, _senor_. He say he
have how you call vision. It tell him you must pay."
records.paraphrase: The priest refuses further aid, saying a vision reveals Hager must pay for his crime.

records.quote: The priest nodded gravely and began his task.
records.paraphrase: A priest attempts to exorcize the supernatural cold.

records.quote:
Even near hot stoves, or in heated rooms, he felt
chilled. No one else seemed to notice it. The cold seemed intended for
him alone.
records.paraphrase: Hager alone feels a cold that others cannot perceive, even in warm places.

records.quote:
If Hager were simply to delay in reaching the settlement, Cahill would
die as surely as though from the thrust of a knife or the impact of a
bullet. Exposure to the biting cold would finish him.
records.paraphrase: Hager reasons that delaying the journey will let exposure to cold kill the sick Cahill without visible marks.

records.quote:
"You're trying to kill me, Matt. I see it
now. You aren't going straight toward Moose Gulch. You're tracking
back and forth to waste time. You ... want me to die!"
records.paraphrase: Cahill realizes and accuses Hager of deliberately stalling to kill him.

records.quote:
"I can't understand it," he told Hager. "There's nothing
seriously wrong with you. All you need is plenty of food and rest.
You're probably just imagining things."
records.paraphrase: A doctor finds no physical cause for Hager's symptoms.

records.quote:
The cold remained with him in the days that followed. It not only
remained. It grew more unbearable.
records.paraphrase: After the murder, an inexplicable cold begins following Hager and worsening.

records.quote:
The climate grew increasingly mild and balmy as he progressed
southward. But the chill that always surrounded him grew worse.
records.paraphrase: Despite traveling to warmer climates, the cold afflicting Hager intensifies.

records.quote: And then he found himself toying with the thought of murdering Cahill.
records.paraphrase: Hager begins contemplating killing his partner.

records.quote:
"You aren't going to get away with this, Matt. I ... I'm going to get
you. I'm going to make you pay."
records.paraphrase: The dying Cahill vows revenge against Hager.

records.quote: It worked.
records.paraphrase: The exorcism temporarily succeeds in relieving Hager.

records.quote:
Several days later found him in Mexico. It was warm--but he didn't
feel it. He knew with a terrible certainty that he would never feel
warmth again.
records.paraphrase: Even in warm Mexico, Hager cannot feel any warmth.

records.quote:
In Los Angeles he yielded to a wild impulse and visited a doctor. He
explained his symptoms, omitting their true cause, and pleaded for
help.
records.paraphrase: Hager seeks a medical examination to explain the cold.

records.quote:
It had been a warm night. The fire had been, hot, the blankets
numerous and thick. Yet Hager had _frozen_ to death.
records.paraphrase: Despite warmth and fire, Hager freezes to death.

records.quote:
It was his plan to keep zigzagging, approaching the
stream and then retreating, always at a tangent. A great deal of time
would be consumed in this way, with very little actual forward
progress toward Moose Gulch.
records.paraphrase: Hager devises a deliberate zigzag route to waste time while appearing to travel.

records.quote:
He was materialistic. He didn't believe in ghosts. But he knew that
he was being haunted by an unnatural cold that nobody else seemed
able to feel.
records.paraphrase: The materialist Hager acknowledges being haunted by an unnatural cold.

criteria.rationale: The story presents no scientific fact, theory, discovery, natural process, or speculative science that is materially represented. The central phenomenon (a vengeful, supernatural cold) is explicitly supernatural rather than scientific; the doctor finds no physical cause and offers no scientific explanation. Ordinary references to cold and exposure are naturalistic backdrop, not represented science.

No device, technique, engineered system, or invention materially affects the setting, problem, action, or outcome. Dogsleds, planes, and trains are ordinary contemporary transportation mentioned in passing and do not constitute speculative or plot-driving technology.

The tale is set in an ordinary contemporary period (Alaska, Seattle, Mexico) with no speculative future, remote past, or temporal displacement. The cited displacement evidence concerns southward spatial travel, not temporal displacement.

The story develops a supernatural retribution premise (a dying man's curse), not consequences extrapolated from an identifiable scientific, technological, social, or historical premise. The unfolding of the cold is a moral/supernatural haunting, not systematic extrapolation of a rational premise.

Hager seeks a medical examination and a doctor performs a complete physical exam attempting to find a cause, which resembles observation and diagnostic inquiry. However, this is a generic medical investigation that yields no findings and does not materially drive understanding or the outcome; the resolution is supernatural (exorcism, curse). Materiality is uncertain, hence ambiguous.

No other planets, dimensions, nonordinary cosmic environments, or visitors from them appear. Alaska and Mexico are ordinary earthly locations. The supernatural cold is a haunting, not a visitor from another realm in the cosmic-environment sense.

The deaths of Cahill and Hager are individual personal misfortunes/supernatural retribution, not a large-scale natural, technological, cosmic, biological, or human-caused disaster. There is no broader scale of catastrophe; the frozen-to-death ending is a single supernatural death, not a mass-casualty or setting-wide calamity.

candidates.description: A supernatural, personalized cold that haunts and ultimately kills the murderer Hager as the fulfillment of his dying partner Cahill's vow of revenge. The cold follows Hager everywhere, cannot be felt by anyone else, intensifies regardless of climate, and finally freezes him to death in a warm room.

novelty.rationale: A cold that is imperceptible to others, intensifies in warm climates, and freezes a man to death in a hot room in Mexico is a totalizing violation of the empirical norm. It transforms the physical laws governing Hager's world into a personalized, agentive force.

cognitive_validation.rationale: The story offers no immanent, systematic, nonsupernatural account of the cold. Medical inquiry finds nothing; the only mechanism that touches it is religious exorcism and a priest's vision of divine retribution, and the cold operates as ghostly vengeance (Cahill's curse). This is an explicitly supernatural/moral-retribution device rather than an imaginary-science or coherent social-organization novum, so cognitive validation fails.

narrative_hegemony.rationale: The vengeful cold governs the entire second half of the narrative: Hager's flight across a continent, his medical and religious attempts at relief, and his final death are all determined by it. It is the overriding narrative logic, not an incidental device.

estrangement.rationale: Readers register the cold against the empirical norm that warm rooms warm people and that others share the same thermal environment; the contrast is sharpened when the materialist Hager, warm-climate Mexico, and a hot fire all fail to produce warmth, culminating in freezing to death on a warm night.

candidates.description: Hager's plan to murder his partner Cahill through calculated delay and exposure, zigzagging the dogsled to waste time so the sick man dies of cold without any visible wound, appearing as a natural death.

novelty.rationale: A murder-by-delayed-exposure scheme is entirely within the empirical norm of a crime story; it introduces no totalizing or world-altering difference from the author's empirical world.

cognitive_validation.rationale: The scheme is coherent and systematically reasoned, but this coherence is that of ordinary criminal planning, not an imaginary science; it is noted only because it is internally consistent.

narrative_hegemony.rationale: The crime drives the first half and motivates everything, but the overriding narrative logic of retribution belongs to the supernatural cold, so the scheme is the precipitating cause rather than the governing novum.

estrangement.rationale: No cognitive estrangement is produced by an ordinary murder plot; it is a mimetic crime device, not a novum.
